newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss parliament set to decide investment plan.
newsitem.headline: Swiss parliament set to decide investment plan.

text.p: Switzerland's parliament will decide next week on a government proposal to revive the stagnant domestic economy with a package of direct investment and corporate tax reforms.

The upper and lower houses have set themselves a deadline to approve the investment side of the package during a special three-day session from Monday through Wednesday called especially to deal with Switzerland's moribund economy.
A vote is expected on Tuesday but could be postponed until Wednesday, when any differences in versions passed by the two houses are to be settled.
"This investment proposal is the reason parliament set this special session and the members firmly intend to pass it," a spokesman for the parliament administration said.
The tax reform side of the bill will also come up for debate but will not be voted on until the next regular parliamentary session from June 2 to 20 or possibly even later.
Driven to act by six years of zero growth, the government hopes to add one-third of a percentage point to gross domestic product in 1998 and 1999.

Under the plan, the federal government would put up 561 million Swiss francs in order to draw matching funds from the country's 26 cantons and thousands of local governments as well as private investors.
The total investment volume should reach 2.4 billion Swiss francs, the government says. It says the spending should be enough to employ 24,000 people.
The focus will be on maintaining public infrastructure, meaning a programme of heavy construction of roads, tunnels and public buildings.
It includes funding for job training for young people and for refitting public and private buildings for energy efficiency.

"By giving a temporary stimulus to demand, the investment programme will accelerate a recovery from economic stagnation which has lasted for six years," the cabinet said in its proposal to parliament.
Swiss GDP was flat in the fourth quarter of 1996, following seven quarters of continued declines. It is expected to grow in 1997 but at less than one percent.
The cabinet's proposed corporate tax reform is more disputed between left and right in the coalition.
The bill would introduce a flat tax rate of 8.5 percent on corporate earnings while abolishing a capital tax now imposed on companies.
It would also lower the issue tax, a one-time levy on the share capital of new companies issuing shares, to one percent from two percent.

To make up for some of the resulting revenue loss, the cabinet want to reintroduce a one-time tax on new life insurance policies, a proposal that is hotly opposed by the country's large insurance sector.

After the new insurance tax, the reforms would still lead to an annual revenue loss of 170 million francs. But the government expects a boost for Swiss businesses that would raise the overall tax base.
